HOOK 1
WAY: Scene first, then the reveal that the rust is the product
MODEL: I1X0kXE34P4
TEXT: On the site of an old steel plant in Weirton, West Virginia, a factory is building batteries filled with pellets of iron. [F5] [F2] Let air reach that iron, and it starts to rust. Nobody stops it.

HOOK 2
WAY: The familiar battery and its flaw, then the rival that fills the gap
MODEL: vUWEXCTmH_w
TEXT: America's new battery runs on rust, and it exists because of one flaw in the batteries we already have. The big lithium batteries on the power grid are fast, and they are proven. [CHECK: that lithium-ion is the main, established battery type on the US grid] But most of them are empty after about four hours.

HOOK 3
WAY: One plain image, then three questions promised by the end
MODEL: D0ZDWvbgCGE
TEXT: America's new battery runs on rust. Inside it, iron meets air and rusts, and that rusting is what gives out the electricity. [F2] Feed power back in, and the rust turns back into iron, ready to go again.

BEATS
BEAT: 1:00 | Name it and pin it down | Names Form Energy, founded in 2017 in Somerville, Massachusetts, with a former Tesla battery chief and an MIT professor among its founders [F1], gives the 26 July 2021 announcement and its "multi-day storage" claim [F3], then the factory of up to $760 million on the former steel-plant site in Weirton, chosen from 50 locations in 16 states [F5] with a state package of up to $290 million [F6], and holds back how rust can make power at all.
BEAT: 2:15 | The strangest part, teased | Says the iron-air idea dates to the 1970s and that the research was abandoned in the 1980s [F19], promises the reason is coming, asks for the like and subscribe, and holds back who built the first one and what stopped it.
BEAT: 3:00 | The four-hour wall | Shows what grid lithium does well and where it stops after a few hours [CHECK: typical duration of grid lithium-ion storage], prices it at around $100 per kWh packaged, as Penn State's Christopher Rahn put it [F14], walks through a windless winter week on a grid full of wind and solar [CHECK: a real example of a long calm, dark spell and how long it lasted], then turns on the fact that Form says its target is to compete with natural gas [F13], so the real rival is the gas plant, and holds back how cheap the battery would have to be.
BEAT: 5:30 | The shelf | Goes back to Westinghouse's R&D Center in Pittsburgh, which built iron-air cells for electric cars under a Department of Energy contract in 1977–78, with cells that passed 100 cycles [F18], pays the "why was it dropped" loop with the research abandoned in the 1980s over "insurmountable technical difficulties" [F19], shows the 2017 revival at Jülich and Oak Ridge, where full batteries lasted only 20 to 30 cycles [F19], the same year Form was founded [F1], and turns on the idea that a battery too heavy for a car may suit a field [CHECK: that weight matters less on the grid, and what Form changed technically; the fact sheet found no page linking Form's design to the 1970s programs], holding back what happens inside one cell.
BEAT: 7:45 | Rust and un-rust | Explains with one household picture, a nail left in the rain, how iron pellets rust when exposed to oxygen to give power and turn back to iron on charge [F2] [CHECK: the chemistry in plain terms and what is inside one cell], and holds back how much energy is lost on every round trip.
BEAT: 9:30 | Proven or promised | Sorts every claim into three piles: built (about 450 workers in May 2025 building the first four batteries, about 40 containers bound for Minnesota [F7]), being built (the 1.5 MW / 150 MWh pilot in Cambridge, Minnesota, ground broken August 2024 [F8], due online in 2027 according to MIT Technology Review [F9] [CHECK: the start date is disputed on the fact sheet; the companies earlier said end of 2025]), and only announced (two Xcel systems of 10 MW for up to 100 hours [F10], the roughly $1 billion Google data center project of 300 MW and 30 GWh for 2028 to 2031 [F11], 12 GWh for Crusoe from 2027 [F17]), then pays the "has it run four days" loop by saying the figure is the company's own "up to 100 hours" [F4] and that no independent field proof was found [CHECK: whether any Form battery is now energized on a grid or has run 100 hours at full power; the research found neither], and holds back what it costs.
BEAT: 12:00 | The price of rust | Sets the 2021 claim of under $20 per kWh against Stanford's Mark Jacobson calling it a "substantial breakthrough" only "if the commercial costs end up that low" [F12], says that as of October 2026 Form had not disclosed its real costs [F13], then pays the Google loop with the outside estimate of about $33 per kWh for that project, in a range of $33 to $50, against lithium at around $100 [F14], and holds back the weak points that price buys.
BEAT: 13:15 | Where it loses | Admits the round-trip efficiency is 40% to 50%, low for a battery and the trade for cheap iron [F15], that it needs roughly one acre per 2 to 3 MW [F16], and that Weirton makes about 2 GWh a year against an 80 GWh backlog [F15] [F16], with about 450 workers in May 2025 against at least 750 jobs expected [F5] [F7], so it wins only the one job of long, cheap, standing storage, and holds back whether the factory can catch up.
BEAT: 14:50 | Back to the factory floor | Returns to the iron pellets in Weirton, says Form raised $750 million for a total of $2 billion since 2017 [F15], names what to watch (the Minnesota system due in 2027 [F9], Crusoe deliveries from 2027 [F17], Google's first phase from 2028 [F11]), and pays the title in full: "for days" is the company's claim of up to 100 hours, about four days [F4], still waiting for its first proof in the field, and the video stops there.
